docs.title: About
docs.text:
In this 3-unit, 8-week graduate course, each student secures one real system from design to production, running on Kubernetes in the department's CloudStack cloud.

Item Detail Course number and name CYB 601 – Software and Systems Security Units 3 Length of class 8 weeks Instructional method Online / On-Campus Expected workload 12–16 hours per week: 3 h class, 3 h reading, 4–5 h lab, 1 h Google Skills lab, 2–3 h discussion and writing. Weeks 4, 7 and 8 run heavier. Recommended preparation Linux command line, Git, one programming language, networking fundamentals. Week 0 covers SSH, the course VPN, kubectl, Terraform and Kubernetes basics.

Description. This course treats security as an engineering discipline: students reason about adversaries, design controls, build them and prove they work. Each student provisions a Kubernetes environment with Terraform on the department's CloudStack cloud, then secures one reference system for eight weeks. They threat-model it, engineer identity and cryptographic controls, and harden the host, the cluster and the container images. They enforce Zero Trust segmentation with a web application firewall, network policy and service-mesh mTLS, and write detections mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. They then build a pipeline that ships only signed, inventoried artifacts. Google Cloud Security Engineer labs run alongside, showing the same controls as managed services. The course ends with a red-team versus blue-team exercise and a security plan defended to technical and executive audiences.

Required text. Anderson, R. (2020). Security Engineering: A Guide to Building Dependable Distributed Systems (3rd ed.). Wiley. Every chapter is free on the author's site; the Perlego edition (eBook ISBN 9781119642817) is optional.

Required standards and papers. NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 1 Rev. 1, SP 800-218 (SSDF), SP 800-63B, SP 800-162, SP 800-207, SP 800-40 Rev. 4, SP 800-92, SP 800-137 and SP 800-204D; OWASP SAMM, ASVS and Top 10; SLSA; MITRE ATT&CK; NIST CSF 2.0. All are free except ISO/IEC 27001 and COBIT, which the library provides. Full list under References.

Required tools. A laptop with a browser, SSH client, Git, VS Code, kubectl and a WireGuard client for the course VPN. OWASP ZAP or Burp Suite Community for the web attacks. A GitHub account and a Google account. Docker Desktop is not required: images build in GitHub Actions and run in the student's own cluster.

docs.title: Connecting to CYB601 Bastion via SSH
docs.text: Your username is pgsXX and your starting password is ChangeMe2026!

docs.title: Step 1: Install cloudflared
docs.text:
Windows (PowerShell):

winget install --id Cloudflare.cloudflared

Close and reopen PowerShell afterwards.

macOS:

brew install cloudflared

Linux (Debian/Ubuntu):

curl -L -o cloudflared.deb <https://github.com/cloudflare/cloudflared/releases/latest/download/cloudflared-linux-amd64.deb>
sudo dpkg -i cloudflared.deb

docs.title: Step 2: Create your SSH config
docs.text:
Windows (PowerShell):

mkdir $HOME\.ssh -Force
notepad $HOME\.ssh\config

Paste this, then save. Make sure the file isn't saved as config.txt.

Host cyb601-bastion
    HostName cyb601.aatizghimire.com.np
    User pgsXX
    ProxyCommand "C:\Program Files (x86)\cloudflared\cloudflared.exe" access ssh --hostname %h

macOS / Linux:

mkdir -p ~/.ssh && chmod 700 ~/.ssh
nano ~/.ssh/config

Paste this, then save with Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X:

Host cyb601-bastion
    HostName cyb601.aatizghimire.com.np
    User pgsXX
    ProxyCommand /usr/local/bin/cloudflared access ssh --hostname %h

Run which cloudflared and use the path it shows. It's often /usr/bin/cloudflared on Linux and /opt/homebrew/bin/cloudflared on Apple Silicon Macs.

docs.title: Step 3: Log in and change your password
docs.text:
ssh cyb601-bastion

Type yes if it asks about the fingerprint, then enter ChangeMe2026!. Nothing appears on screen while you type, which is normal.

Once you're in, change your password right away:

passwd

Then type exit to log out.

docs.title: Step 4: Generate your SSH key (on your own computer)
docs.text:
The command is the same on all systems:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519

Press Enter to accept the default location. You can set a passphrase for extra safety or press Enter twice to skip it.

This creates two files in your .ssh folder:

  • id_ed25519 is your private key. Never share it with anyone.
  • id_ed25519.pub is your public key, and that's the one that goes on the server.

docs.title: Step 5: Upload your public key
docs.text:
macOS / Linux:

ssh-copy-id cyb601-bastion

Windows (PowerShell):

type $HOME\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub | ssh cyb601-bastion "mkdir -p ~/.ssh && chmod 700 ~/.ssh && cat >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys"

Enter your new password when asked.

docs.title: Step 6: Test it
docs.text:
ssh cyb601-bastion

You should log in without a password prompt (or only your key passphrase, if you set one). You're done! 🎉

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
"no such host": Flush your DNS cache and try again.

OS Command Windows ipconfig /flushdns macOS sudo dscacheutil -flushcache Linux resolvectl flush-caches

"Permission denied" with your password: Check that Caps Lock is off and type the password carefully, including the !.

Still asked for a password after Step 5: The key didn't upload. Repeat Step 5.

docs.title: CYB 601 – Starter Repository (GitHub scaffold)
docs.text:
Also, Available at https://github.com/PGS-CYB/cyb601-template .

This is the cyb601-<lastname> template students fork in Week 0. Create a new GitHub repository from these files, mark it a template, and add the instructor as a collaborator. Files marked TODO are the ones you finalize for your Proxmox environment before term.

docs.title: How to use this scaffold
docs.text:
Each section below is one file in the repository. Copy its contents into the path shown in the heading. When every file is in place:

  1. Create a new GitHub repository named cyb601-template, private, owned by the course org.
  2. Commit these files, then in Settings mark the repository as a template.
  3. In Week 0, students choose "Use this template" to create their own cyb601-<lastname>, add you as a collaborator, and work in it all term.

What you finalize before term (every TODO):

  • infra/terraform.tfvars.example: your Proxmox node name, template VM ID, pool and bridge.
  • app/: the customer API image (the base ships a stub) and your mock customer dataset.
  • .github/workflows/ci.yaml: the Cosign identity string for your org, and the registry path.

Two planted weaknesses stay in the base on purpose, so the labs have something to find:

  • An over-permissive ServiceAccount binding in app/api/ (students fix it in Lab 3).
  • A plaintext database password in app/data/ (gitleaks finds it in Lab 4).

docs.title: README.md
docs.text:
# CYB 601 – Software and Systems Security

Your working repository for the term. You provision one Kubernetes environment
on the course Proxmox server, then secure one reference system across seven labs.

## Prerequisites (Week 0)

- An SSH client, Git, VS Code, `kubectl`, Terraform or OpenTofu, and `jq`.
- Access to the course Proxmox URL and the public bastion (your instructor sends both).
- A GitHub account and a Google account (for the Google Skills labs).

Run the environment check with your bastion details:

```bash
BASTION=BASTION_IP BASTION_USER=BASTION_USER ./tools/week0-check.sh | tee week0/check.txt

docs.title: Reaching your environment
docs.text:
• Proxmox console: https://PROXMOX_URL:8006
  • Bastion (SSH jump host): ssh BASTION_USER@BASTION_IP
  • Your VM, through the bastion: ssh -J BASTION_USER@BASTION_IP ubuntu@VM_IP
  • Your cluster, from your laptop: tunnel the API, then use kubectl 
    ssh -J BASTION_USER@BASTION_IP -f -N -L 6443:127.0.0.1:6443 ubuntu@VM_IP
export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/cyb601.yaml
kubectl get nodes

Student VMs have no public address. Everything in reaches you through the bastion; the cluster only calls out (DNS and 443) for images, GitHub and signature checks.

docs.title: Provisioning (Week 1)
docs.text:
cd infra
cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars   # then edit the values
export PROXMOX_VE_ENDPOINT="https://PROXMOX_URL:8006"
read -rs PROXMOX_VE_API_TOKEN; export PROXMOX_VE_API_TOKEN   # user@realm!id=secret
terraform init
terraform plan -out=lab1.tfplan
terraform apply lab1.tfplan

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: Path What it is infra/ Terraform for your VM and k3s (bpg/proxmox provider) app/ The reference system: Juice Shop, a customer API, Postgres, a WAF placeholder tools/ The Week 0 environment check .github/workflows/ The Lab 4 image build and the Lab 7 security pipeline labs/ Your evidence and reports, one folder per lab

docs.title: Submitting a lab
docs.text:
Commit your work, then tag it:

git add labs/labN
git commit -m "Lab N: <summary>"
git push
git tag labN-submit && git push origin labN-submit

Then upload the 2-page report PDF to the LMS. See labs/README.md.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Attack only your own VM and cluster; in the capstone, only your assigned target.
  • Never scan or test anything outside the course Proxmox environment.
  • Keep secrets out of Git. If one is exposed, rotate it, then clean history.
  • AI tools may explain errors and syntax; analysis and conclusions are your own and are disclosed in each lab's README.

docs.title: infra/ Terraform (bpg/proxmox)
docs.text:
infra/versions.tf

terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5"
  required_providers {
    proxmox = {
      source  = "bpg/proxmox"
      version = "~> 0.81"
    }
  }
}

# Credentials come from PROXMOX_VE_ENDPOINT and PROXMOX_VE_API_TOKEN
# in your environment, never from this file.
provider "proxmox" {
  insecure = false
}

infra/variables.tf

variable "name"           { type = string }  # lab-LASTNAME
variable "node"           { type = string }  # the Proxmox node name
variable "template_id"    { type = number }  # the course template's VM ID
variable "pool"           { type = string }  # your resource pool
variable "ssh_public_key" { type = string }  # your public key, from Week 0
variable "k3s_version"    { type = string }  # pinned by your instructor

variable "bridge"    { type = string, default = "vmbr1" }
variable "cores"     { type = number, default = 2 }
variable "memory_mb" { type = number, default = 6144 }
variable "disk_gb"   { type = number, default = 50 }

infra/main.tf

# Upload cloud-init as a Proxmox snippet (enable the "snippets" content
# type on the local datastore first).
resource "proxmox_virtual_environment_file" "cloud_init" {
  content_type = "snippets"
  datastore_id = "local"
  node_name    = var.node
  source_raw {
    data      = templatefile("${path.module}/cloud-init.yaml.tftpl", { k3s_version = var.k3s_version })
    file_name = "${var.name}-cloud-init.yaml"
  }
}

resource "proxmox_virtual_environment_vm" "lab" {
  name      = var.name
  node_name = var.node
  pool_id   = var.pool

  clone { vm_id = var.template_id }   # the course Ubuntu 24.04 template

  cpu    { cores = var.cores }
  memory { dedicated = var.memory_mb }

  disk {
    datastore_id = "local-lvm"
    interface    = "scsi0"
    size         = var.disk_gb
  }

  network_device { bridge = var.bridge }
  agent          { enabled = true }

  initialization {
    datastore_id      = "local-lvm"
    user_data_file_id = proxmox_virtual_environment_file.cloud_init.id
    ip_config { ipv4 { address = "dhcp" } }
    user_account {
      username = "ubuntu"
      keys     = [trimspace(var.ssh_public_key)]
    }
  }
}

output "vm_ip" {
  # requires the guest agent; [1][0] is the first real NIC's address
  value = proxmox_virtual_environment_vm.lab.ipv4_addresses[1][0]
}

infra/terraform.tfvars.example — copy to terraform.tfvars and fill in. Contains no secrets, so the example is committed.

name           = "lab-LASTNAME"
node           = "NODE_NAME"      # TODO: your Proxmox node
template_id    = 9000             # TODO: the course template's VM ID
pool           = "POOL_NAME"      # TODO: your resource pool
ssh_public_key = "ssh-ed25519 AAAA... you@example.edu"
bridge         = "vmbr1"          # TODO: the student network bridge
k3s_version    = "K3S_VERSION"    # TODO: pinned by your instructor

docs.title: infra/cloud-init.yaml.tftpl
docs.text:
Installs k3s on first boot and gives the ubuntu user a private kubeconfig. The ${k3s_version} placeholder is filled by Terraform.

#cloud-config
package_update: true
packages:
  - jq
  - nmap
write_files:
  - path: /etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml
    content: |
      # Lab 4 adds hardening settings here (audit log, etc.).
      write-kubeconfig-mode: "0600"
runcmd:
  - curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io -o /root/install-k3s.sh
  - INSTALL_K3S_VERSION="${k3s_version}" sh /root/install-k3s.sh
  - mkdir -p /home/ubuntu/.kube
  - cp /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml /home/ubuntu/.kube/config
  - chown -R ubuntu:ubuntu /home/ubuntu/.kube
  - chmod 600 /home/ubuntu/.kube/config
  - echo 'export KUBECONFIG=$HOME/.kube/config' >> /home/ubuntu/.bashrc

docs.title: tools/week0-check.sh
docs.text:
Mark it executable before committing: git update-index --chmod=+x tools/week0-check.sh. One of terraform or tofu will report missing; that is expected.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prints tool versions and connectivity for the Week 0 environment check.
set -u
echo "== Tools =="
for cmd in git ssh kubectl terraform tofu jq; do
  if ! command -v "$cmd" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "$cmd: missing"
    continue
  fi
  case "$cmd" in
    ssh)       echo "ssh: $(ssh -V 2>&1)" ;;
    kubectl)   echo "kubectl: $(kubectl version --client 2>/dev/null | head -n 1)" ;;
    terraform) echo "terraform: $(terraform version | head -n 1)" ;;
    tofu)      echo "tofu: $(tofu version | head -n 1)" ;;
    *)         echo "$cmd: $("$cmd" --version 2>&1 | head -n 1)" ;;
  esac
done
echo "== Connectivity =="
BASTION="${BASTION:?set BASTION to the bastion address}"
BASTION_USER="${BASTION_USER:-$USER}"
if ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5 -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new \
     "$BASTION_USER@$BASTION" true 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "SSH to bastion: ok"
else
  echo "SSH to bastion: FAILED"
fi
if ssh -T -o ConnectTimeout=5 -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new git@github.com 2>&1 \
     | grep -q "successfully authenticated"; then
  echo "GitHub SSH: ok"
else
  echo "GitHub SSH: FAILED"
fi
echo "Checked at $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) by $(git config user.name 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)"

app/shop/deployment.yaml — OWASP Juice Shop. It runs as root by default, which Lab 4's restricted Pod Security forces you to fix.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: juice-shop, namespace: shop }
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: juice-shop } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: juice-shop } }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: juice-shop
          image: bkimminich/juice-shop:v17.1.1   # pin a version; update as needed
          ports: [{ containerPort: 3000 }]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: juice-shop, namespace: shop }
spec:
  selector: { app: juice-shop }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 3000 }]

app/data/postgres.yaml — holds the mock customer records. PLANTED WEAKNESS: the password is in plaintext in the manifest; gitleaks finds it in Lab 4, and you move it into a Secret with k3s encryption.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: postgres, namespace: data }
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: postgres } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: postgres } }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:16
          env:
            - name: POSTGRES_DB
              value: customers
            - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
              value: "Sup3rSecret-ChangeMe"   # PLANTED: plaintext secret (Lab 4)
          ports: [{ containerPort: 5432 }]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: postgres, namespace: data }
spec:
  selector: { app: postgres }
  ports: [{ port: 5432, targetPort: 5432 }]

app/api/deployment.yaml — TODO: replace the stub image with your customer API. The stub just proves the namespace and wiring.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: customer-api, namespace: api }
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: customer-api } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: customer-api } }
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: customer-api
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: hashicorp/http-echo:1.0   # TODO: replace with the real API
          args: ["-text=customer-api stub", "-listen=:8080"]
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: customer-api, namespace: api }
spec:
  selector: { app: customer-api }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]

app/api/rbac.yaml — PLANTED WEAKNESS: the customer API's ServiceAccount is bound to a cluster role that can read every Secret in the cluster. Students find and fix this in Lab 3.

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata: { name: customer-api, namespace: api }
---
# PLANTED: far more access than a web API needs. Replace with a least-
# privilege Role in Lab 3.
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata: { name: customer-api-too-much }
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: view        # cluster-wide read, including Secrets in many setups
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: customer-api
    namespace: api

app/waf/placeholder.yaml — a pass-through so the edge exists from Week 1; Lab 5 replaces it with Nginx + ModSecurity + the OWASP Core Rule Set.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: waf, namespace: waf }
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: waf } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: waf } }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: waf
          image: nginx:stable   # Lab 5: swap for an image with ModSecurity + CRS
          ports: [{ containerPort: 80 }]

docs.title: .github/workflows/
docs.text:
.github/workflows/lab4-build.yaml — builds and pushes the hardened image from Lab 4. Students extend this into the full pipeline in Lab 7.

name: lab4-build
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    paths: ["lab4/Dockerfile", ".github/workflows/lab4-build.yaml"]
permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: lab4
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/juice-shop:hardened

.github/workflows/ci.yaml — the Lab 7 pipeline. Each stage fails the build on a serious finding; fill the TODO identity before enforcing signing.

name: ci
on: [pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write
  id-token: write        # for Cosign keyless signing
jobs:
  secrets:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - uses: gitleaks/gitleaks-action@v2

  sast:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: returntocorp/semgrep-action@v1
        with: { config: p/default }

  deps-and-iac:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Trivy filesystem
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.28.0
        with: { scan-type: fs, severity: "HIGH,CRITICAL", exit-code: "1" }
      - name: Checkov (IaC)
        uses: bridgecrewio/checkov-action@v12
        with: { directory: . }

  build-scan-sign:
    needs: [secrets, sast, deps-and-iac]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - name: Build
        id: build
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: lab4
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/juice-shop:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Trivy image scan
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.28.0
        with:
          image-ref: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/juice-shop:${{ github.sha }}
          severity: "CRITICAL"
          exit-code: "1"
      - name: SBOM (Syft, CycloneDX)
        uses: anchore/sbom-action@v0
        with:
          image: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/juice-shop:${{ github.sha }}
          format: cyclonedx-json
          output-file: sbom.cdx.json
      - name: Cosign keyless sign + attest SBOM
        uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@v3
      - run: |
          cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/juice-shop:${{ github.sha }}
          cosign attest --yes --predicate sbom.cdx.json --type cyclonedx \
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/juice-shop:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Conftest policy gate
        uses: instrumenta/conftest-action@master
        with: { files: lab7/evidence, policy: lab7/policy }

  dast:
    needs: [build-scan-sign]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: ZAP baseline
        uses: zaproxy/action-baseline@v0.12.0
        with: { target: "http://localhost:3000" }   # TODO: start the container first

In Lab 7, students replace the permissive Cosign identity with their workflow's exact --certificate-identity / --certificate-oidc-issuer, and Kyverno verifies the same identity at admission.

labs/README.md

# Labs

One folder per lab (`lab1/` through `lab7/`), plus `week0/` for the setup check.
Each folder holds the evidence the lab asks for and a `README.md` written from
the `_TEMPLATE.md` below.

## Submitting

```bash
git add labs/labN
git commit -m "Lab N: <summary>"
git push
git tag labN-submit && git push origin labN-submit

Then upload the 2-page report PDF to the LMS. Grading uses the engineering lab rubric: working implementation (14), evidence (8), analysis and risk reasoning (12), professional communication (6).

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• The lab must rebuild from a clean clone using this README.
  • Keep secrets out of Git. Report any exposed secret within 24 hours.
  • Disclose any AI use; analysis and conclusions are your own. 
    **`labs/_TEMPLATE.md`** — copy into each `labN/README.md`.

```markdown
# Lab N – <title>

## What I built
<one paragraph>

## How to run it
<commands to reproduce from a clean clone>

## Evidence
<command output, configs, scan results — or links to the files in this folder>

## Analysis
<answers to the lab's questions; link findings to the threat model and readings;
state the residual risk>

## What failed and how I fixed it
<short note>

## AI use
<what you used it for, if any>

That completes the scaffold. Drop these files into a repo, mark it a template, and you're ready for Week 0.

docs.title: Course learning outcomes and alignment
docs.text:
The eight CLOs keep the original wording word for word; each now has a week that teaches it and a graded artifact that assesses it.

# Course learning outcome PLOs Taught Assessed by 1 Analyze software/service architectures (enterprise, cloud, container/K8s) to identify security dependencies, weaknesses, and design risks. 1 Wk 1 Lab 1, Final 2 Apply security frameworks (e.g., NIST SSDF, OWASP SAMM/ASVS, NIST SP 800-160, Zero Trust) to produce secure system designs. 1, 2 Wk 1, 2, 5 Lab 2, Lab 5, Final 3 Perform threat modeling (STRIDE, attack trees) and risk analysis to inform requirements, design, and controls. 2, 3 Wk 2 Lab 2, Final 4 Author a secure design specification demonstrating defense-in-depth, least privilege, and secure-by-design principles. 2, 3 Wk 4 Lab 4, Summative 1 5 Engineer authN/authZ, cryptographic protections, secrets, keys, and data-at-rest/in-transit controls aligned to business risk. 3, 4 Wk 3, 4, 5 Lab 3, Lab 4, Lab 5 6 Instrument systems for observability (logs, metrics, traces) and implement runtime protections (policy as code, WAF/Armor, Binary Authorization). 3, 4 Wk 5, 6, 7 Lab 5 (WAF), Lab 6 (logs, metrics, traces, runtime detection), Lab 7 (admission control, the open-source equivalent of Binary Authorization) 7 Establish DevSecOps verification (SAST/DAST/IAST, IaC scanning, artifact integrity, SBOM, supply-chain controls) and document evidence. 3, 4 Wk 7 Lab 7, Summative 2 8 Present and defend software/system security design and verification results to both technical and executive audiences. 1–4 Wk 8 Capstone debrief, Final presentation and defense

IAST is covered conceptually in Week 7 and in Summative 2's coverage analysis rather than as a tool exercise.

docs.title: Lab environment and running case study
docs.text: All seven labs run on one CloudStack server with 128 GB RAM, 32 CPU cores and 2 TB of storage. That fits 15 students at one 6 GB single-node Kubernetes cluster each, plus shared class services.

docs.title: Running case study
docs.text:
Students are the security engineering team for a fictional retailer taking its web shop to production. The system is OWASP Juice Shop plus a small customer API and its Postgres database, deployed to each student's own k3s cluster. Each lab's output feeds the next: the Week 2 threat model decides what Week 5 blocks and what Week 6 detects, and the final plan cites all seven labs.

lab architecture · one of 15 student VMs shown

Students enter only through the VPN; clusters call the internet only for code, images and signature checks.

docs.title: What runs in each student cluster
docs.text:
Namespace Runs Added in kube-system k3s, CoreDNS, Traefik (k3s's bundled ingress) Lab 1 shop OWASP Juice Shop Lab 1 api, data Customer API and the Postgres database holding mock customer records Lab 1 identity Keycloak and oauth2-proxy Lab 3 cert-manager Internal certificate authority and certificates Lab 4 waf Nginx with ModSecurity and the OWASP Core Rule Set Lab 5 istio-system Istio in ambient mode Lab 5 falco, observability Falco and Grafana Alloy Lab 6 kyverno, flux-system Kyverno admission control and Flux GitOps Lab 7

The instructor's dry run confirms that the full stack, with a ZAP scan running, fits in 6 GB before the term starts.

docs.title: Network and access
docs.text:
• Students reach their VM only through the course WireGuard VPN or the SSH bastion. Only the VPN endpoint has a public address.
  • Security groups block traffic between student VMs. The instructor opens red-team-to-target paths only during the capstone.
  • Outbound traffic is limited to DNS and TCP 80/443, and it is logged. Clusters need it to pull images, reach GitHub and check Sigstore signatures.
  • Images build in GitHub Actions, and from Lab 7 Flux pulls deployments from GitHub. Nothing on the internet ever connects into a cluster.

docs.title: Provisioning
docs.text: Each student gets a CloudStack account with an API key and a limit of one VM, 2 vCPU, 6 GB RAM, 50 GB disk and one snapshot. In Week 1 they write Terraform with the proxmox provider to create that VM, and cloud-init installs k3s. Terraform code and Kubernetes manifests are graded like any other code, and Checkov scans them in Lab 7.

docs.title: Tool stack by lab
docs.text: Lab Tools Provisioning Terraform, cloud-init, Ansible, kubectl, Kustomize 1 nmap, Syft, kube-bench 2 OWASP Threat Dragon 3 Keycloak, oauth2-proxy, ZAP or Burp Suite, Kubernetes RBAC 4 OpenSCAP or Lynis, Ansible, kube-bench, Pod Security Admission, Trivy, cert-manager, testssl.sh, gitleaks, k3s secrets encryption 5 ZAP, Nginx with ModSecurity and the OWASP Core Rule Set, NetworkPolicy, Istio ambient mode 6 Grafana Alloy with its Beyla eBPF component, Falco, Sigma with the pySigma Loki backend; the class Loki, Tempo, Prometheus and Grafana 7 GitHub Actions, gitleaks, Semgrep, Trivy, Checkov, ZAP baseline, Syft, Cosign, Conftest, Flux, Kyverno Capstone Caldera or Atomic Red Team

docs.title: Rules
docs.text: Item Rule Repository One private GitHub repository per student, cyb601-lastname, with a folder per lab plus Terraform and manifests. The instructor is a collaborator; commit history is evidence. Rebuildable Every lab must rebuild from a clean clone using its README. The instructor rebuilds a random sample each week. Ethics and scope Students attack only their own VM, and in the capstone only their assigned target. Touching the CloudStack host, bastion, class services or a classmate's VM is an integrity violation and may be illegal. A rules-of-engagement form is signed in Week 1 and re-signed before the capstone. Internet use Outbound access is for packages, images, GitHub and signature checks. Scanning any outside system is prohibited. AI tools Allowed for explaining errors and tool syntax. Analysis, risk ratings and conclusions are the student's own, and AI use is disclosed in the lab README. Living plan From Week 2, each student keeps SECURITY-PLAN.md in the repository and extends it after each lab. Week 8 assembles the final plan rather than starting it.

docs.title: Week 1 – Foundations: thinking like a security engineer
docs.text:
Students learn Anderson's frame of policy, mechanism, assurance and incentives, then provision their own environment and map its attack surface. CLO 1.

Readings

  • Anderson (2020), Ch. 1 "What Is Security Engineering?" and Ch. 2 "Who Is the Opponent?"
  • NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 1 Rev. 1 (2022), Chapters 1–2
  • Saltzer and Schroeder (1975), "The Protection of Information in Computer Systems", Section I.A.3 (design principles)

Discussion. Pick one breach from the last three years that has a public post-incident report. Was the root cause a software security failure, a system security failure or an incentive failure in Anderson's sense? Name the one Saltzer and Schroeder principle that would have changed the outcome, and the lifecycle stage where it should have been applied.

Hands-on Lab 1: Provision, deploy and map the attack surface (40 pts, about 4 h)

  1. Write Terraform with the CloudStack provider, starting from the course module, that creates your VM from the course template; cloud-init installs k3s. Commit the code and the terraform plan output.
  2. Deploy the reference system from the starter repository with Kustomize: Juice Shop, the customer API, Postgres and a pass-through placeholder for the WAF.
  3. Inventory the system: namespaces, Services and ports, ServiceAccounts and RBAC bindings, images and data stores. Generate an SBOM for every image with Syft.
  4. Scan your VM with nmap from the bastion, then from inside a pod. Explain why the two views differ.
  5. Run kube-bench with its k3s benchmark and record the score as the baseline you will improve in Lab 4.
  6. Draw a data-flow diagram with trust boundaries, entry points and assets, including the CloudStack API, the bastion and GitHub.
  7. Rank the five assets an attacker would want most, and name the opponent from Anderson Ch. 2 who would want each.
  8. Sign and commit the rules of engagement.

Deliverable: lab1/ with the Terraform code, data-flow diagram, inventory, SBOMs, kube-bench baseline and a one-page architecture risk memo.

Additional assignment: Google Skills lab (20 pts). A Tour of Google Cloud Hands-on Labs. Badge plus a 3–5 sentence reflection comparing Google Cloud's project and IAM boundaries with the CloudStack account and project boundaries you used in Lab 1.

docs.title: Week 2 – Secure SDLC and threat modeling
docs.text:
Students turn the Week 1 diagram into a threat model and derive testable security requirements from it. CLOs 2 and 3.

Readings

  • Anderson (2020), Ch. 27 "Secure Systems Development"
  • NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (current version)
  • OWASP SAMM v2 model overview; OWASP ASVS (current version), chapter list and levels
  • Threat Modeling Manifesto (2020)

Discussion. Microsoft SDL and OWASP SAMM prescribe practices; BSIMM measures what firms actually do. For a 15-developer startup shipping weekly, which would you adopt first, and which three practices would you start with? Support the choice with one breach where a missing SDLC practice was the documented cause.

Hands-on Lab 2: STRIDE threat model, attack tree and risk register (40 pts, about 4 h)

  1. Rebuild the Lab 1 data-flow diagram in OWASP Threat Dragon.
  2. Apply STRIDE per element. Record at least 15 threats, each with the asset affected and the trust boundary crossed.
  3. Include at least three threats against the platform itself: the Kubernetes API, the CloudStack API keys and the CI pipeline.
  4. Build one attack tree for the highest-value asset, at least three levels deep, with cost or skill on the leaves.
  5. Rate each threat on a 5 × 5 likelihood-impact matrix and justify the top five ratings.
  6. Write a testable security requirement for each of the top ten threats, mapped to an ASVS requirement and an SSDF practice.
  7. Start SECURITY-PLAN.md with the system description and the top risks.

Deliverable: lab2/ with the Threat Dragon JSON and report, the attack tree and a risk register in CSV. The register is reused in Labs 5, 6 and 7, the capstone and the final plan.

Additional assignment: Google Skills lab (20 pts). Implement Cloud Security Fundamentals on Google Cloud. Badge plus reflection: which STRIDE categories do IAM roles and service accounts mitigate, and which do they not touch?

docs.title: Week 3 – Identity and access control engineering
docs.text:
Students break access control first, then rebuild it with a standards-based identity provider and least-privilege Kubernetes RBAC. CLO 5.

Readings

  • Anderson (2020), Ch. 6 "Access Control"
  • NIST SP 800-63B, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication (current revision), authenticator assurance levels
  • NIST SP 800-162, Guide to Attribute Based Access Control, Sections 1–2
  • ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A controls 5.15–5.18 (access control, identity management, authentication information, access rights)
  • OWASP Top 10, Broken Access Control
  • Kubernetes documentation, "Role Based Access Control Good Practices"

Discussion. RBAC is the enterprise default, yet role explosion pushes large organizations toward ABAC or relationship-based models. Using one recent incident involving privilege escalation or over-permissioned identities, argue which model would have limited the damage. Include where DAC and MAC still fit.

Hands-on Lab 3: OIDC, Kubernetes RBAC and broken access control (40 pts, about 4 h)

  1. Attack: from your laptop over the VPN, use ZAP or Burp to solve three Juice Shop broken-access-control challenges, such as viewing another user's basket, reaching the admin section or forging a JWT. Record the request, response and root cause for each.
  2. Build: configure Keycloak in your cluster with a realm, two roles (customer, admin), two users and an OIDC client using authorization code flow with PKCE. Require a one-time-password second factor for the admin role.
  3. Enforce: put oauth2-proxy in front of the customer API so that /admin needs the admin role. Show an allowed and a denied request with the decoded tokens.
  4. Test the tokens: an expired token, a tampered signature and alg: none. Record what is rejected and why.
  5. Platform identity: the starter repository grants one workload far more Kubernetes access than it needs. Find it, replace it with a least-privilege Role, and prove the change with kubectl auth can-i.
  6. Write an access control matrix (subjects × resources × actions) covering application users and platform identities, and mark every cell that violates least privilege.

Deliverable: lab3/ with the Keycloak realm export (secrets removed), oauth2-proxy and RBAC manifests, attack write-ups and the access matrix.

Additional assignment: Google Skills lab (20 pts). Managing Security in Google Cloud. Badge plus reflection: how do Cloud Identity and the resource hierarchy express the matrix you wrote in Lab 3?

docs.title: Week 4 – Hardening, patching, cryptography and secrets
docs.text:
Students measure the host, the cluster and the images against baselines, fix them as code, and fix how the system handles keys and secrets. CLOs 4 and 5.

Readings

  • Anderson (2020), Ch. 5 "Cryptography": read for what engineers must get right; the mathematics can be skimmed
  • CIS Benchmarks for Ubuntu Linux and for Kubernetes, Level 1 (free with registration); the k3s CIS hardening guide
  • Kubernetes documentation, "Pod Security Standards" and "Encrypting Confidential Data at Rest"
  • NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 4 (2022), Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Planning
  • U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform (2018), The Equifax Data Breach, executive summary and patch management findings

Discussion. Equifax had a patch policy and a vulnerability scanner, yet ran a known-vulnerable Apache Struts for months. Using the House report, identify the two process failures that mattered most. Then state a patch SLA you would defend for internet-facing systems, and what you would do when a patch cannot be applied in that time.

Hands-on Lab 4: Host, cluster and image hardening, TLS and secrets (40 pts, about 5 h)

Optional: snapshot your VM before you start, and delete the snapshot after you submit. Your one snapshot slot is needed before the capstone.

  1. Host: scan your VM with OpenSCAP and the CIS profile for your Ubuntu release, or with Lynis. Record the score and the ten highest-risk findings.
  2. Write an Ansible playbook that fixes at least eight of them, rescan, and show before and after.
  3. Cluster: rerun kube-bench and fix at least five findings in the k3s configuration, including API audit logging (Lab 6 uses that log). Compare against your Lab 1 baseline.
  4. Workloads: label the application namespaces to enforce the "restricted" Pod Security Standard. Fix every violation: non-root user, read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped, seccomp RuntimeDefault, no privilege escalation.
  5. Images: scan the Juice Shop image with Trivy. Write a hardened Dockerfile on a minimal base, build it with the starter repository's build workflow, rescan and compare CVE counts.
  6. Transport: issue certificates from an internal CA with cert-manager and terminate TLS at Traefik. Test with testssl.sh and remove every weak protocol and cipher it reports.
  7. Secrets: run gitleaks over the repository history and remove the database password planted in the starter manifests. Move it into a Kubernetes Secret, turn on k3s secrets encryption, and show the stored value is ciphertext in the datastore. Then rotate the encryption key.

Deliverable: lab4/ with before-and-after reports for host, cluster and image; the playbook, k3s configuration diff, Dockerfile and namespace labels; the TLS report; the encryption evidence; and a list of findings deliberately not fixed, each with a reason.

Summative Assessment 1: System Hardening Report (60 pts, 3–4 pages, APA 7). A secure design specification for the hardened host, cluster and workloads, written from the Lab 4 evidence. Required sections: baselines chosen and why; defense-in-depth layers with the control at each; least-privilege decisions; before-and-after metrics; exceptions with compensating controls and a named risk owner; patch management policy with SLAs by severity; key and secret lifecycle, including rotation. CLO 4.

Additional assignment: Google Skills lab (20 pts). Mitigating Security Vulnerabilities on Google Cloud. Badge plus reflection linking vulnerability management to software resilience.

docs.title: Week 5 – Network and application defense, Zero Trust
docs.text:
Students put a WAF in front of the application and measure what it stops, then enforce Zero Trust inside the cluster with network policy and mesh identity. CLOs 2, 5 and 6.

Readings

  • Anderson (2020), Ch. 21 "Network Attack and Defence" and Ch. 7 "Distributed Systems" (selected sections)
  • NIST SP 800-207 (2020), Zero Trust Architecture, Sections 2–3
  • Ward and Beyer (2014), "BeyondCorp: A New Approach to Enterprise Security"
  • OWASP Top 10 (current edition)
  • Istio documentation, ambient mode overview and "Ambient and Kubernetes NetworkPolicy"

Discussion. Critics say Zero Trust is a rebranding of least privilege and network segmentation. Using SP 800-207's tenets and one documented deployment, such as Google BeyondCorp or the U.S. federal strategy in OMB M-22-09, argue what is new and what is not. Then place a WAF, a NetworkPolicy and a mesh authorization policy in the 800-207 logical model, and say what each cannot see.

Hands-on Lab 5: WAF, network policy and service-mesh mTLS (40 pts, about 5 h)

  1. Baseline: run a ZAP active scan plus manual SQL injection, XSS and path traversal against Juice Shop. Save the alerts.
  2. WAF: replace the Lab 1 placeholder with Nginx, ModSecurity and the OWASP Core Rule Set in detection-only mode. Replay the attacks and read the audit log.
  3. Switch to blocking at paranoia level 1, then 2. Record blocked attacks and false positives on normal shopping traffic at each level.
  4. Tune: write one rule exclusion for a false positive, and one custom rule for a Lab 2 threat that the Core Rule Set misses.
  5. Segment: apply default-deny NetworkPolicies to every application namespace, then allow only the flows in your data-flow diagram. Prove it with allowed and blocked requests from a test pod, and repeat the Lab 1 in-pod nmap scan.
  6. Mesh: install Istio in ambient mode with the starter values file and enroll the application namespaces. Traffic will break until your NetworkPolicies allow port 15008; explain why.
  7. Enforce strict mTLS, and write authorization policies so that only the API's service account can reach Postgres and only the WAF can reach Juice Shop. Prove each with an allowed and a denied request, and show the workload certificate on a live connection.

Deliverable: lab5/ with configs and policies, before-and-after scans, a table of blocked versus missed attacks, the policy test evidence, and the residual risks that a WAF and a mesh cannot address.

Additional assignment: Google Skills lab (20 pts). Securing Your Network with Cloud Armor. Badge plus reflection: compare Cloud Armor's preconfigured rules and bot management with your ModSecurity deployment. What does the managed service give you, and what control do you lose?

docs.title: Week 6 – Observability and detection engineering
docs.text:
Students send logs, metrics and traces from every layer to the class observability stack, add runtime detection, and measure how well their detections work. CLO 6.

Readings

  • Anderson (2020), Ch. 28 "Assurance and Sustainability"
  • NIST SP 800-137 (2011), Information Security Continuous Monitoring, Sections 2–3
  • NIST SP 800-92, Guide to Computer Security Log Management (current revision), Sections 2–4
  • MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise and Containers matrices: Initial Access, Credential Access and Exfiltration tactics
  • Sigma rule specification (SigmaHQ) and the Falco rules documentation

Discussion. In the 2013 Target breach the malware alerts fired and nobody acted; in 2020 FireEye found the SolarWinds intrusion from a single unusual device registration. Using both cases, argue whether the harder engineering problem is collecting telemetry or acting on it. Propose two metrics a security lead should report monthly to show detection is improving.

Hands-on Lab 6: Telemetry, runtime detection and ATT&CK-mapped rules (40 pts, about 5 h)

  1. Logs: with Grafana Alloy, ship application logs, Traefik access logs, ModSecurity audit logs, Keycloak authentication events and the Lab 4 Kubernetes audit log to your tenant in the class stack.
  2. Metrics and traces: enable Alloy's Beyla component for Juice Shop and the customer API. Send RED metrics to the class Prometheus and traces to the class Tempo, then follow one admin API request from its trace to its log lines.
  3. Runtime: deploy Falco with its modern eBPF probe. Enable or write rules for a shell spawned in a container, an unexpected outbound connection, a write below a read-only path and a read of a service-account token.
  4. Detections: pick five threats from the Lab 2 register. Write each as a Sigma rule tagged with its ATT&CK technique, convert it to LogQL with the pySigma Loki backend, and load it as an alert in your tenant. At least one detection must use a metric or trace signal.
  5. Replay the Lab 3 and Lab 5 attacks plus 10 minutes of normal traffic. For each rule, record fired or missed, time to alert and false positives.
  6. Build one dashboard with four panels an on-call engineer would need, and write a half-page triage runbook for the noisiest alert.
  7. Threat-model your own telemetry: Alloy and Falco run with elevated privileges. Add their risks and mitigations to your register.

Deliverable: lab6/ with the Sigma rules and generated LogQL, Falco rules, Alloy configuration, dashboard JSON, a detection coverage table (threat, technique, rule, result) and the runbook.

Additional assignment: Google Skills lab (20 pts). Logging and Monitoring in Google Cloud. Badge plus reflection on which of your detections could be built with Cloud Logging and log-based alerts, and which assurance metrics you would report.

docs.title: Week 7 – DevSecOps and software supply chain security
docs.text:
Students build a pipeline that ships only scanned, signed and inventoried images, and a cluster that refuses anything else. CLOs 6 and 7.

Readings

  • Anderson (2020), Ch. 8 "Economics" (why vendors ship insecure software and who pays)
  • OWASP DevSecOps Guideline, pipeline stages overview
  • SLSA specification (current version), build track levels
  • NIST SP 800-204D (2024), Strategies for the Integration of Software Supply Chain Security in DevSecOps CI/CD Pipelines, Sections 3–5
  • Sigstore documentation on keyless signing; Kyverno documentation on image verification
  • Case files: SolarWinds (2020), Log4Shell (2021), the xz-utils backdoor (2024)

Discussion. SolarWinds compromised the build, Log4Shell was a flaw in a trusted dependency, and xz-utils was a maintainer takeover. For each, state which control (SAST, SCA, SBOM, signing, provenance, admission control, reproducible builds) would have prevented or shortened it, and which would have done nothing. Conclude with what automation cannot fix.

Hands-on Lab 7: Signed pipeline, GitOps and admission control (40 pts, about 5 h)

  1. Extend the starter build workflow in GitHub Actions to run on every pull request, in this order: gitleaks, Semgrep (SAST), Trivy filesystem scan (dependencies), Checkov on your Terraform and Kubernetes manifests (IaC), image build, Trivy image scan, and a ZAP baseline against the container in the runner (DAST).
  2. Generate a CycloneDX SBOM with Syft and attach it to the image as an attestation.
  3. Sign the image and the SBOM attestation with Cosign keyless signing. Show cosign verify passing, then failing on a tampered image.
  4. Pipeline policy: write a Conftest (Rego) policy that fails the build on any critical CVE, a root user or a missing SBOM. Show one red build and one green build.
  5. GitOps: install Flux in your cluster and point it at your repository. The pipeline updates the image digest by pull request and Flux deploys it, so nothing connects into the cluster.
  6. Admission: install Kyverno. Write policies that admit only images signed by your repository's workflow, require a non-root user and resource limits, and generate a default-deny NetworkPolicy in every new namespace. Show one deployment rejected and one admitted.
  7. Triage: from all findings, pick ten, classify each as true positive, false positive or accepted risk, and fix at least three in code.

Deliverable: lab7/ with the workflow YAML, Rego and Kyverno policies, the SBOM, Flux configuration, links to the red and green runs, rejection evidence and the triage table.

Summative Assessment 2: DevSecOps Risk and Verification Report (60 pts, 4–5 pages, APA 7). An evidence-backed assessment of the Lab 7 pipeline and deployment path. Required sections: pipeline architecture and trust boundaries; verification coverage by stage against SSDF practices, including what IAST would add; findings triage with risk ratings; SBOM analysis (riskiest components, license issues); artifact integrity, the SLSA build level achieved and the gap to the next; the admission gate as the last line of defense; residual risk and a 90-day improvement plan. CLO 7.

Additional assignment: Google Skills lab (20 pts). Using DevSecOps in Your Google Cloud Environment. Badge plus reflection comparing Artifact Registry scanning and Binary Authorization with your Trivy, Cosign and Kyverno gates.

docs.title: Week 8 – Governance, risk communication and the red/blue capstone
docs.text:
Students test their systems against a live red team, then assemble seven weeks of evidence into one plan and defend it to two audiences. CLO 8, integrating CLOs 1–7.

Readings

  • Anderson (2020), Ch. 27, sections on organizational issues (re-read), and Ch. 29 "Beyond 'Computer Says No'"
  • NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (2024), the Govern function
  • ISACA, COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology, governance overview
  • ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Clauses 5, 6 and 9 (leadership, planning, performance evaluation)

Discussion. You have budget for one of three things next year: a second detection engineer, a developer security champions program, or a commercial tool replacing your open-source pipeline scanners. Choose one for the case-study retailer and defend it to the CFO in plain language, with one metric that would prove you right in 12 months. Use your capstone results as evidence.

docs.title: Capstone: red team versus blue team (Week 8 live session; counts as Week 8 participation, 20 pts)
docs.text:
• Targets. Twenty-four hours before the session, the instructor randomly picks one member's cluster per blue team and restores it from that student's pre-capstone snapshot. Everyone therefore keeps their own cluster ready.
  • Teams and rounds. The class forms four teams of three or four. Two engagements run in parallel, then teams swap roles, so every student plays red once and blue once. Each round lasts 60 minutes, followed by a 30-minute joint debrief.
  • Red starting point. The public URL, one low-privilege shop account, and a shell in a pod in the shop namespace, simulating a compromised dependency.
  • Red objectives. Read mock customer records in Postgres, steal a service-account token, persist or escalate in the cluster, and exfiltrate data, using Caldera or Atomic Red Team plus manual technique. Every action is logged with a timestamp and its ATT&CK technique.
  • Blue rules. Detect, contain and evict using only the controls built in Labs 3–7. Policies may change during the round; new tools may not be installed.
  • Out of scope. Denial of service, the CloudStack host and its API, the bastion, the class services and any cluster not assigned as a target. Rules of engagement are re-signed before the session.
  • Scoring. Red scores on objectives reached and time taken. Blue scores on time to detect, time to contain and detection coverage. The debrief reconciles the red timeline against the blue team's alerts to find the gaps.
  • Cannot attend live. Within 48 hours, replay the red team's recorded Caldera operation against your own cluster and reconcile it against your alerts, for the same participation points.

Within 48 hours, each student writes a one-page after-action note: what their side did, what worked, what the other side did that they missed, and the two highest-priority fixes. It becomes the capstone section of the final plan.

docs.title: Final Project: Comprehensive Software and Systems Security Plan and Presentation (140 pts)
docs.text:
The plan covers the student's own system as built in Labs 1–7 and tested in the capstone. It is assembled from SECURITY-PLAN.md, which students have extended since Week 2.

Part A, written plan (8–10 pages plus evidence appendix, APA 7, 90 pts)

  • Executive summary: one page, no jargon, top three risks and the ask
  • System architecture and threat model summary
  • Software lifecycle controls mapped to SSDF and SAMM
  • IAM model and network defense
  • Monitoring and incident detection, with Lab 6 coverage results
  • DevSecOps automation and supply chain integrity
  • Governance and compliance: control mapping to NIST CSF 2.0 and ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A
  • Residual risk register with owners, and a 12-month improvement roadmap with metrics
  • Capstone findings (20 of the 90 points): the after-action note, the reconciled timeline and the changes it drove
  • Appendix: a link to repository evidence for every claim

Part B, presentation and defense (10–12 slides, 50 pts)

  • A 12-minute presentation in two parts: 4 minutes to an executive audience (risk, cost, decision needed) and 8 minutes to a technical audience (architecture, evidence, trade-offs).
  • Then 5 minutes of questions from the instructor and two assigned peer reviewers. Students who present by recording answer written questions within 48 hours.

Submit both parts to the LMS by Sunday of Week 8.

docs.title: Week 0 – Prerequisites and environment setup
docs.text: Week 0 gets every student onto the lab cloud, GitHub and Kubernetes before graded work starts. Nothing this week is graded, but every lab from Week 1 assumes it is done.

docs.title: Assignment: readiness check
docs.text:
Week 0 carries no points. Complete all four parts before the Week 1 live session.

Part 1 – Self-assessment. Tick what you can already do; anything left unticked is your Week 0 study list.

  • SSH to a server with a key and copy files with scp
  • Read a service log with journalctl and find a listening port with ss
  • Clone, branch, commit, push and tag with Git
  • Explain a /24 network, a port and a DNS lookup
  • Read and edit YAML without breaking the indentation
  • Write a 20-line script in one programming language

Part 2 – Prerequisite quiz. Answer each question in a few lines in week0/quiz.md. Fewer than 7 correct means booking extra time at the environment check.

  1. What does chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 do, and why does SSH care?
  2. How many usable host addresses does 10.20.0.0/24 have?
  3. What are the default ports for SSH, DNS and HTTPS?
  4. What is the difference between git commit and git push?
  5. You pushed an API key to GitHub five minutes ago. What do you do first, and why?
  6. What is the difference between a container image and a running container?
  7. What does a Kubernetes Service give you that a Pod's IP address does not?
  8. What does terraform plan show, and why should someone review it before apply?
  9. What does a reverse proxy do? Name one security control it can enforce.
  10. Why is curl https://example.com/install.sh | sh risky? Give two safer options.

Part 3 – Introduce yourself on the discussion board. In about 150 words: your security background, one system you have been responsible for, and one thing you want to be able to do by Week 8. Reply to two classmates.

Part 4 – Submit your environment check. Finish Hands-on Lab 0, then push week0/check.txt, week0/quiz.md and week0/notes.md, and the tag week0-submit.

docs.title: Hands-on Lab 0: Set up and touch the cloud (ungraded, about 3 h)
docs.text:
By the end, you have every tool installed, reach the lab cloud through the public bastion, have run Kubernetes on a throwaway VM, and have pushed your first tagged commit.

Your instructor sends you the bastion address and username, your Proxmox URL and username, and the template repository link. Replace the UPPERCASE placeholders below with those values.

docs.title: Step 1 – Install the tools on your laptop
docs.text:
Tool Used for Install from Git Version control git-scm.com VS Code Editing code and YAML code.visualstudio.com kubectl Talking to Kubernetes kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tools Terraform or OpenTofu Infrastructure as code developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/install or opentofu.org SSH client SSH to the bastion and your VM Built in on macOS, Linux and WSL jq Reading JSON output jqlang.github.io/jq

On Windows, run wsl --install in an administrator terminal, then do all command-line work in the Ubuntu shell it creates. Install VS Code on Windows itself.

git --version
kubectl version --client
terraform version      # or: tofu version
ssh -V
jq --version

docs.title: Step 2 – Create an SSH key
docs.text:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.edu"
ls -l ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

The private key must show -rw-------. Share only the .pub file: add it to GitHub under Settings, SSH and GPG keys, and submit it through the course key form so the bastion lets you in.

docs.title: Step 3 – Reach the public bastion
docs.text:
The bastion has a public address, so you connect to it directly over SSH; there is no VPN.

Add the bastion to ~/.ssh/config:

Host cyb601-bastion
    HostName BASTION_IP
    User BASTION_USER
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

ssh cyb601-bastion hostname

Check: the bastion prints its hostname. If it does not, use the troubleshooting table at the end.

docs.title: Step 4 – Sign in to Proxmox and create an API token
docs.text:
1. Open your Proxmox console at https://PROXMOX_URL:8006, sign in and change your password.
  2. Upload your SSH public key where your instructor directs (you also add it through cloud-init in Lab 1), named LASTNAME-key.
  3. In Datacenter, then Permissions, then API Tokens, create a token for your user. Store the token ID and secret in a password manager, never in a file inside your repository.
  4. Load them into your shell without echoing them or saving them in history:
export PROXMOX_VE_ENDPOINT="https://PROXMOX_URL:8006"
printf 'API token (user@realm!id=secret): '; read -rs PROXMOX_VE_API_TOKEN; echo; export PROXMOX_VE_API_TOKEN

These variables vanish when the terminal closes, which is the point. Week 1's first terraform plan is the real test of the keys.

docs.title: Step 5 – Build a practice VM by clicking
docs.text:
1. In Proxmox, clone a VM from the course Ubuntu 24.04 template. Give it 2 vCPU and 6 GB, attach the student network, and add your SSH public key through the template's cloud-init. Name it practice-LASTNAME.
  2. Note its IP address; it is VM_IP below.
  3. Write down every choice you made in the console. In Week 1 you rewrite them as Terraform.
  4. Connect through the bastion:
ssh -J cyb601-bastion ubuntu@VM_IP

docs.title: Step 6 – Kubernetes in 30 minutes
docs.text:
On the practice VM, download the k3s installer, read it, then run it:

curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io -o install-k3s.sh
less install-k3s.sh
sudo sh install-k3s.sh

Give your user a private copy of the cluster credentials:

mkdir -p ~/.kube
sudo cp /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml ~/.kube/config
sudo chown "$USER" ~/.kube/config
chmod 600 ~/.kube/config
echo 'export KUBECONFIG=$HOME/.kube/config' >> ~/.bashrc
export KUBECONFIG=$HOME/.kube/config
kubectl get nodes

Deploy, expose and break something:

kubectl create namespace practice
kubectl -n practice create deployment web --image=nginx:stable
kubectl -n practice expose deployment web --port=80
kubectl -n practice get pods,svc -o wide
kubectl -n practice run curl --rm -it --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -s http://web
kubectl -n practice scale deployment web --replicas=3
kubectl -n practice delete pod -l app=web --wait=false
kubectl -n practice get pods -w        # Ctrl+C once all three are Running again
kubectl -n practice exec deploy/web -- id
kubectl -n practice logs deploy/web --tail=20

Answer these in week0/notes.md:

  1. Why did the pods come back after you deleted them?
  2. Which user does nginx run as inside the container, and why will that fail Week 4's restricted policy?
  3. Who can read /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml, and what could someone do with it?
  4. Why read install-k3s.sh before running it as root?

docs.title: Step 7 – See the site from your laptop
docs.text:
ssh -J cyb601-bastion -L 8080:localhost:8080 ubuntu@VM_IP \
  'kubectl --kubeconfig ~/.kube/config -n practice port-forward svc/web 8080:80'

Open http://localhost:8080. You are seeing nginx through two tunnels: SSH to the VM, then kubectl to the Service. Press Ctrl+C to close both.

docs.title: Step 8 – Create your course repository
docs.text:
1. On GitHub, open the template repository, choose "Use this template", and create a private repository named cyb601-LASTNAME. Add your instructor as a collaborator.
  2. Clone it on your laptop and run the environment check:
git clone git@github.com:YOUR_GITHUB_USER/cyb601-LASTNAME.git
cd cyb601-LASTNAME
mkdir -p week0
BASTION=BASTION_IP BASTION_USER=BASTION_USER ./tools/week0-check.sh | tee week0/check.txt
  1. Add quiz.md and notes.md to week0/, then commit, push and tag:
git add week0/
git commit -m "Week 0: environment check, quiz and notes"
git push
git tag week0-submit
git push origin week0-submit

docs.title: Step 9 – Clean up
docs.text: Destroy practice-LASTNAME in Proxmox (stop it, then remove), and confirm it is gone from the VM list. Your quota allows one VM, and Week 1 needs it.

docs.title: Week 1 – Foundations: thinking like a security engineer
docs.text: Week 1 teaches to think like security engineers, then has them build their own cluster in code and map its attack surface. CLO 1.

docs.title: Slides of Week 1
docs.text: Week-1 Slide

docs.title: Assignments
docs.text: Week 1 has four pieces of work: the discussion, the rules of engagement, the Google Skills lab and Lab 1. All are due by Sunday at 11:59 p.m. Pacific, except the primary discussion post, due Thursday.

docs.title: Discussion (20 pts)
docs.text:
Prompt. Pick one breach from the last three years that has a public post-incident report. Was the root cause a software security failure, a system security failure or an incentive failure in Anderson's sense? Name the one Saltzer and Schroeder principle that would have changed the outcome, and the lifecycle stage where it should have been applied.

What a full-marks post does

  • Links the post-incident report and summarizes the attack path in three or four sentences.
  • Classifies the root cause with evidence from the report, not adjectives.
  • Names exactly one principle, the mechanism that would have applied it, and the lifecycle stage.
  • Cites at least one primary source beyond Anderson, in APA 7, in at least 200 words.
  • Replies to two classmates (50 words or more each) with new evidence or a reasoned challenge to their classification.

docs.title: Rules of engagement (required before any scan in Lab 1)
docs.text:
Copy this into lab1/rules-of-engagement.md, fill in your name and the date, and commit it. A typed name counts as your signature unless your instructor asks for a signed PDF.

# CYB 601 rules of engagement

I, NAME, agree that for the whole course I will:

1. Test only systems assigned to me: my own VM and cluster, and in the capstone only my assigned target.
2. Not scan, probe or attack anything outside the course cloud, including from my VM.
3. Not access the Proxmox host or console, any account but my own, the bastion beyond my login, the class services, or a classmate's VM.
4. Not run denial-of-service tests against shared infrastructure.
5. Keep secrets out of Git, and report any secret I expose or discover within 24 hours.
6. Report suspected incidents or out-of-scope access to the instructor at once.

I understand that breaking these rules is an academic integrity violation and may be illegal.

Signed: NAME
Date: YYYY-MM-DD

docs.title: Google Skills lab (20 pts)
docs.text: A Tour of Google Cloud Hands-on Labs. Upload the completion badge or summary screen showing your name, plus 3–5 sentences: compare Google Cloud's project and IAM boundaries with the Proxmox user and token scope you used in Lab 1. Where is the trust boundary in each, and who can cross it?

docs.title: Lab 1 submission (40 pts)
docs.text:
• Push your work and the tag lab1-submit.
  • Upload a 2-page lab report PDF to the LMS: what you built, the evidence, your analysis of the two nmap views and the kube-bench baseline, and what failed and how you fixed it.
  • Grading uses the engineering lab rubric: working implementation 14, evidence 8, analysis 12, communication 6.

docs.title: Hands-on Lab 1: Provision, deploy and map the attack surface (40 pts, about 4 h)
docs.text:
You rebuild last week's practice VM as code, deploy the reference system, and produce the inventory, scans, baseline and diagram that every later lab builds on.

Before you start: Bastion reachable; Proxmox token loaded in this terminal (Lab 0, step 4); practice VM removed; Syft installed on your laptop; rules of engagement committed.

docs.title: Part A – Provision your VM with Terraform (about 1 h)
docs.text:
Your repository's infra/ folder holds the starter module. Complete it so it matches these files.

infra/versions.tf

terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5"
  required_providers {
    proxmox = {
      source  = "bpg/proxmox"
      version = "~> 0.81"
    }
  }
}

# Credentials come from PROXMOX_VE_ENDPOINT and PROXMOX_VE_API_TOKEN
# in your environment, never from this file.
provider "proxmox" {
  insecure = false
}

infra/variables.tf

variable "name"           { type = string }  # lab-LASTNAME
variable "node"           { type = string }  # the Proxmox node name
variable "template_id"    { type = number }  # the course template's VM ID
variable "pool"           { type = string }  # your resource pool
variable "ssh_public_key" { type = string }  # your public key, from Week 0
variable "k3s_version"    { type = string }  # pinned by your instructor

variable "bridge"    { type = string, default = "vmbr1" }
variable "cores"     { type = number, default = 2 }
variable "memory_mb" { type = number, default = 6144 }
variable "disk_gb"   { type = number, default = 50 }

infra/main.tf

# Upload your cloud-init as a Proxmox snippet (needs the "snippets"
# content type enabled on the local datastore).
resource "proxmox_virtual_environment_file" "cloud_init" {
  content_type = "snippets"
  datastore_id = "local"
  node_name    = var.node
  source_raw {
    data      = templatefile("${path.module}/cloud-init.yaml.tftpl", { k3s_version = var.k3s_version })
    file_name = "${var.name}-cloud-init.yaml"
  }
}

resource "proxmox_virtual_environment_vm" "lab" {
  name      = var.name
  node_name = var.node
  pool_id   = var.pool

  clone { vm_id = var.template_id }   # the course Ubuntu 24.04 template

  cpu    { cores = var.cores }
  memory { dedicated = var.memory_mb }

  disk {
    datastore_id = "local-lvm"
    interface    = "scsi0"
    size         = var.disk_gb
  }

  network_device { bridge = var.bridge }
  agent          { enabled = true }

  initialization {
    datastore_id      = "local-lvm"
    user_data_file_id = proxmox_virtual_environment_file.cloud_init.id
    ip_config { ipv4 { address = "dhcp" } }
    user_account {
      username = "ubuntu"
      keys     = [trimspace(var.ssh_public_key)]
    }
  }
}

output "vm_ip" {
  value = proxmox_virtual_environment_vm.lab.ipv4_addresses[1][0]
}

infra/cloud-init.yaml.tftpl

#cloud-config
package_update: true
packages:
  - jq
  - nmap
write_files:
  - path: /etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml
    content: |
      # Lab 4 adds hardening settings here.
      write-kubeconfig-mode: "0600"
runcmd:
  - curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io -o /root/install-k3s.sh
  - INSTALL_K3S_VERSION="${k3s_version}" sh /root/install-k3s.sh
  - mkdir -p /home/ubuntu/.kube
  - cp /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml /home/ubuntu/.kube/config
  - chown -R ubuntu:ubuntu /home/ubuntu/.kube
  - chmod 600 /home/ubuntu/.kube/config
  - echo 'export KUBECONFIG=$HOME/.kube/config' >> /home/ubuntu/.bashrc

infra/terraform.tfvars holds the values your instructor publishes. It contains no secrets, so it is committed.

name           = "lab-LASTNAME"
node           = "NODE_NAME"
template_id    = 9000                               # the course template's VM ID
pool           = "POOL_NAME"
ssh_public_key = "ssh-ed25519 AAAA... you@example.edu"
bridge         = "vmbr1"
k3s_version    = "K3S_VERSION"

Your .gitignore must contain these lines. Commit .terraform.lock.hcl: it pins the provider's checksums, a supply-chain control you meet again in Week 7. Never commit state, which can hold sensitive values.

.terraform/
*.tfstate
*.tfstate.*
*.tfplan

Plan, read the plan, then apply it:

cd infra
terraform init
terraform fmt -check
terraform validate
terraform plan -out=lab1.tfplan
mkdir -p ../lab1
terraform show -no-color lab1.tfplan > ../lab1/terraform-plan.txt
terraform apply lab1.tfplan
VM_IP=$(terraform output -raw vm_ip)
ssh -J cyb601-bastion ubuntu@"$VM_IP" 'cloud-init status --wait && kubectl --kubeconfig ~/.kube/config get nodes'

Check: the node reports Ready. In your report, name one line of the plan you would challenge if a teammate had written it.

docs.title: Part B – Reach the cluster from your laptop and deploy (about 30 min)
docs.text:
scp -J cyb601-bastion ubuntu@"$VM_IP":.kube/config ~/.kube/cyb601.yaml
chmod 600 ~/.kube/cyb601.yaml
ssh -J cyb601-bastion -f -N -L 6443:127.0.0.1:6443 ubuntu@"$VM_IP"
export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/cyb601.yaml
kubectl get nodes

That kubeconfig is full cluster-admin. Keep it outside your repository, readable only by you. Then, from your repository root:

kubectl apply -k app/
kubectl get pods -A -w        # Ctrl+C when every pod is Running

docs.title: Part C – Inventory and SBOMs (about 45 min)
docs.text:
kubectl get ns > lab1/namespaces.txt
kubectl get deploy,sts,ds,svc,ingress -A -o wide > lab1/workloads.txt
kubectl get sa,roles,rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A > lab1/identities.txt
kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{range .spec.containers[*]}{.image}{"\n"}{end}{end}' \
  | sort -u > lab1/images.txt

mkdir -p lab1/sbom
while read -r img; do
  syft "$img" -o cyclonedx-json > "lab1/sbom/$(echo "$img" | tr '/:@' '___').cdx.json"
done < lab1/images.txt

for f in lab1/sbom/*.json; do echo "$(jq '.components | length' "$f") $f"; done | sort -rn

In your report, answer: which image carries the most packages? Which data store holds customer records, and who can reach it? Which service account can do more than it needs? Lab 3 fixes that last one.

docs.title: Part D – Scan from two places (about 30 min)
docs.text:
From the bastion, scan every port on your VM. Then scan every pod from inside the cluster.

ssh cyb601-bastion "nmap -sT -Pn -p- $VM_IP" > lab1/nmap-from-bastion.txt

PODS=$(kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.podIP}')
kubectl run scan --rm -i --quiet --restart=Never --image=instrumentisto/nmap -- \
  -sT -Pn -p 1-10000 $PODS > lab1/nmap-from-pod.txt

In your report, explain why the two results differ and which flows Lab 5 should block.

docs.title: Part E – CIS baseline with kube-bench (about 20 min)
docs.text:
On the VM:

KB=KUBE_BENCH_VERSION    # pinned by your instructor, without the leading v
curl -sLO "https://github.com/aquasecurity/kube-bench/releases/download/v${KB}/kube-bench_${KB}_linux_amd64.tar.gz"
sudo mkdir -p /opt/kube-bench
sudo tar -xzf "kube-bench_${KB}_linux_amd64.tar.gz" -C /opt/kube-bench
ls /opt/kube-bench/cfg | grep -i k3s
sudo /opt/kube-bench/kube-bench run \
  --config-dir /opt/kube-bench/cfg --config /opt/kube-bench/cfg/config.yaml \
  --benchmark K3S_BENCHMARK > kube-bench-baseline.txt
grep -A 5 "Summary total" kube-bench-baseline.txt

Then, on your laptop:

scp -J cyb601-bastion ubuntu@"$VM_IP":kube-bench-baseline.txt lab1/

docs.title: Part F – Data-flow diagram (about 45 min)
docs.text:
Draw it in OWASP Threat Dragon, which you reuse in Lab 2, or in draw.io. Save the image and the source file in lab1/. Include:

  • External entities: customer browser, admin, GitHub, the Proxmox API, the bastion
  • Processes: Traefik, the WAF placeholder, Juice Shop, the customer API
  • Data stores: Postgres, Juice Shop's internal database, the k3s datastore, Terraform state on your laptop
  • Flows: HTTP and HTTPS, SQL, kubectl, SSH, Terraform API calls
  • Trust boundaries: internet to VPN, bastion to VM, edge to application, application to data, cluster to outside, your laptop to the control plane

docs.title: Part G – Assets and opponents (about 20 min)
docs.text: Rank Asset Where it lives Opponent (Anderson Ch. 2) What they want with it 1 Customer records Postgres, data namespace Crooks Resale and payment fraud 2 3 4 5

docs.title: Part H – Memo and submission
docs.text:
Write lab1/risk-memo.md: one page with your top three architecture risks, the evidence for each, and what you would fix first. Then:

git add infra/ lab1/
git commit -m "Lab 1: provisioned VM, inventory, scans, baseline, DFD"
git push
git tag lab1-submit
git push origin lab1-submit

  • lab1/nmap-from-bastion.txt and lab1/nmap-from-pod.txt
  • lab1/kube-bench-baseline.txt
